content.text: DRY, as Andy Hunt and Dave Thomas define it, says every piece of knowledge needs one authoritative representation in a system. It's about duplicated knowledge, not duplicated text. Two blocks of code can look identical and encode different rules, so merging them couples things that should change separately, while the same business rule can hide in code that looks nothing alike.
. A month ago a reviewer merged

, because the two bodies were identical. The developer widens its pattern, coupons work, and signup quietly starts accepting usernames with hyphens and up to 30 characters. The same week, free shipping moves from 50 to 75. The cart is updated, but the banner computes "amount left" with its own 50, so a customer with 60 in the cart is told shipping is free and then charged for it. Two bugs, opposite causes: one merge too many and one too few.
The belief: DRY means any two pieces of code that look alike must be merged into one shared function, base class or utility. If a duplicate-code check flags it, extract it.

It's an easy belief to pick up. Copy-paste detectors in CI report similar lines, not similar intent. Code review rewards spotting repetition. And the authors themselves admit the first edition of The Pragmatic Programmer "did a poor job" of explaining DRY: many readers took it to mean "don't copy-and-paste lines of source." In a 2003 interview Dave Thomas called DRY "probably one of the most misunderstood parts of the book."
The half-truth: copy-pasted code often is duplicated knowledge, and removing it is valuable. But Hunt and Thomas call it "a tiny and fairly trivial part" of DRY.

, as the 20th anniversary edition states it: "Every piece of knowledge must have a single, unambiguous, authoritative representation within a system." In the interview Thomas lists what knowledge includes: code, but also database schemas, test plans, the build system and documentation. The reason is practical: when the same thing is expressed in several places, the copies fall out of step. Or, in the book's words, "It isn't a question of whether you'll remember: it's a question of when you'll forget."
The acid test is change, not appearance

The book gives a test: when a single facet of the code has to change, do you find yourself making that change "in multiple places, and in multiple different formats?" If so, the code isn't DRY. Notice what the test looks at: what happens when a rule changes, not whether two lines look alike.

The book's own example is a wine shop that validates a customer's age and an order quantity. Both must be numbers greater than zero, so the two functions are identical, and a reviewer calls it a DRY violation. The authors disagree: "The code is the same, but the knowledge they represent is different." The two rules just happen to match today: "That's a coincidence, not a duplication." Merging them turns a

: the next change to one rule silently changes the other. Microsoft's architecture guide makes the same point about two constants that share a value but mean different things, and concludes: "Duplication is always preferable to coupling to the wrong abstraction."

The more dangerous duplication rarely looks like duplication. The book describes DRY as being about expressing the same thing "possibly in two totally different ways": a rule in code and again in a comment, in a schema and in the class that mirrors it. In the hook,
share no text at all, so no detector will ever flag them, yet they encode one business fact.

None of this makes DRY weaker. Martin Fowler wrote in 2001 that the principle is simply to "say anything in your program only once", and that a determined effort to remove repetition leads a long way toward good design. He also notes that coincidental duplication exists, but finds it "rare and easy to spot". Kent Beck's rules of simple design include "no duplication", which Beck phrased as saying things "Once and only Once". The skill is aiming the principle at knowledge.
The fix: one home per fact, not per shape

tabs.label: ❌ Wrong
✅ Right

content.text: The two validators are separate again, even though they still look similar, because the account team and marketing will change them for different reasons. The shipping threshold, which looked like two unrelated expressions, now lives in one constant that both functions read. If finance moves it to 100, that's a one-line change, and the banner can't disagree with the cart.

rows.text: DRY means one authoritative representation per piece of knowledge
Identical code can encode different rules; Hunt and Thomas call that a coincidence
Code that looks different can't be duplicated
One business rule can hide in code, comments, schemas and SQL that share no text
A duplicate-code tool finds DRY violations
It finds repeated text; only the change test finds repeated knowledge
Thomas: knowledge includes schemas, test plans, the build and documentation

content.text: Before merging two look-alike blocks, ask: "If this rule changes, must the other copy change too, every time?" If the answer is yes, merge them. If it's "maybe" or "it depends who asks", leave them apart; you can still extract a lower-level helper both use, like a regex builder, without tying the two rules together.

blocks.title: A shared helper that grows flags is coupling to the wrong abstraction

content.text: When every new caller adds a boolean or an optional parameter (
), the helper has stopped representing one piece of knowledge. Each change now risks every caller. Inline it back into the callers, let them diverge, and look again for what is truly shared.
How to apply it in your project

items.title: Triage duplicate-code warnings with the change test

content.text: For each flagged pair, decide whether one rule changing must always change the other. Merge true duplicates; mark coincidences so the next reviewer doesn't merge them.

items.title: Hunt for duplicates that don't look alike

content.text: Search for business numbers and names across layers: thresholds, rates, limits, status names. Check the frontend, the backend, SQL, configuration and docs.

items.title: Give each fact one authoritative home

content.text: Put it in one constant, table or config value, and derive the rest from it. For schemas and APIs, Hunt and Thomas suggest generating code from one source, such as a database schema or an OpenAPI spec.
Where a shared helper has collected flags, copy it back into each caller, delete the flags, and let each version follow its own rule.

items.text: DRY means every piece of knowledge has one authoritative representation, not "no similar-looking code".
Identical code can encode different rules; merging it couples changes that should stay separate.
The worst duplication often looks nothing alike: the same rule in different code, schemas or docs.
Judge duplication by change: if one copy changing must always change the other, it's one piece of knowledge.
A shared helper that keeps growing flags is a sign the abstraction was wrong; un-merging it is a valid refactoring.
